about.title: Rancho Cucamonga Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Getting hurt at work in Rancho Cucamonga usually starts a workers' compensation claim, and for many people that is where it ends. California law makes workers' comp the exclusive remedy against your employer regardless of fault. What often goes unnoticed is the second question: did someone other than your employer contribute to the injury? A subcontractor on a job site, a property owner who ignored a hazard, a company that built faulty equipment, or another driver on I-15 or SR-210 while you were making a work run can each be responsible in a separate claim. Those third-party claims carry a two-year deadline and can cover losses workers' comp does not. We handle workplace injury cases in San Bernardino County and review both workers' compensation and third-party claims. We work on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery. Report the injury to your employer within 30 days, then contact us to review whether a second path applies to you.

items.question: I was hit on Foothill Boulevard while driving for work. Is that just a workers' comp case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. If you were on the clock, workers' comp should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of fault. If another driver caused the crash, you may also have a separate injury claim against that driver, which follows California's two-year deadline. Rancho Cucamonga recorded 474 injury collisions in 2025, with reports peaking on Fridays between 5 and 7 p.m., so work-related crashes on Foothill Boulevard, I-15, and SR-210 are not unusual.

items.question: Do I have to report my injury right away?
items.answer: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days. Reporting sooner is better, because it starts your workers' comp claim and creates a record of what happened. Your employer cannot legally retaliate against you for reporting.

items.question: Can I sue my employer if the injury was their fault?
items.answer: In most cases, no. Workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against an employer in California, even when the employer was careless. The separate claim comes into play when a third party, such as a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker, shares responsibility. We can review whether that applies to your situation.
